clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder of lysine degradation caused by deficiency of the bifunctional enzyme alpha-aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase (AASS), which carries both lysine-ketoglutarate reductase and saccharopine dehydrogenase activities.

Widely regarded as a benign biochemical variant rather than a true disease; most individuals are ascertained incidentally on plasma amino acid analysis or newborn screening follow-up and are neurologically normal.

Two biochemical patterns exist: a combined defect of both enzyme activities (classic hyperlysinaemia) and an isolated saccharopine dehydrogenase defect producing saccharopinuria; both stem from mutations in the single AASS gene.
Hallmark biochemistry is a markedly raised plasma lysine, with saccharopine and homocitrulline sometimes detectable, distinguishing it from other causes of a high lysine.
Reported neurodevelopmental or ophthalmological findings in early case series are now largely attributed to ascertainment bias or coincidental conditions rather than to the metabolic defect itself.
Because lysine catabolism is impaired proximal to glutaryl-CoA, hyperlysinaemia does not produce the encephalopathic crises or glutaric acid accumulation seen in glutaric aciduria type 1.
No specific treatment or dietary lysine restriction is generally required; counselling to reassure families of the benign nature is the mainstay.

Distinguish from secondary hyperlysinaemia due to urea cycle disorders (particularly hyperlysinaemia accompanying pyruvate carboxylase deficiency or generalised aminoaciduria) before labelling it primary.
reference.pathophysiology: Hyperlysinaemia results from biallelic loss-of-function variants in AASS on chromosome 7, which encodes alpha-aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase, a mitochondrial bifunctional enzyme mediating the first two committed steps of the saccharopine pathway of lysine degradation. Its N-terminal lysine-ketoglutarate reductase domain condenses lysine with 2-oxoglutarate to form saccharopine, and its C-terminal saccharopine dehydrogenase domain then converts saccharopine to alpha-aminoadipic semialdehyde and glutamate. When both activities are deficient, lysine accumulates in blood, cerebrospinal fluid and urine; when only the dehydrogenase domain is affected, saccharopine accumulates and spills into urine (saccharopinuria). Because the block lies upstream of alpha-aminoadipate and glutaryl-CoA, no neurotoxic organic acids accumulate, which underlies the generally benign clinical course. The saccharopine pathway is the principal route of lysine catabolism in most tissues, and the enzyme deficiency leaves the pipecolic-acid pathway as an alternative minor route.
additionalDifferentials: Saccharopinuria (isolated saccharopine dehydrogenase defect, allelic AASS variant)
Glutaric aciduria type 1 (downstream lysine-pathway defect with encephalopathic crises)
Hyperprolinaemia (another benign amino acidopathy sometimes found incidentally)
Pyroglutamic aciduria and other benign incidental aminoacidurias
Secondary hyperlysinaemia from urea cycle disorders or generalised aminoaciduria
Pyruvate carboxylase deficiency (can produce raised lysine among other amino acids)
additionalInvestigations: Quantitative plasma amino acid analysis demonstrating isolated marked elevation of lysine
Urine amino acid and organic acid analysis to detect saccharopine, homocitrulline and to exclude organic aciduria
Cerebrospinal fluid amino acids in selected cases to confirm central elevation
Plasma ammonia and urea cycle intermediates to exclude secondary hyperlysinaemia
AASS gene sequencing to confirm the diagnosis and clarify combined versus isolated enzyme defect
Enzyme activity assay of lysine-ketoglutarate reductase and saccharopine dehydrogenase in cultured fibroblasts where available
redFlags: Coexisting encephalopathy, seizures or developmental regression should prompt a search for an alternative or additional diagnosis rather than attribution to hyperlysinaemia
Hyperammonaemia suggests a urea cycle disorder causing secondary lysine elevation
Metabolic acidosis or an abnormal organic acid profile points to a downstream lysine catabolic defect
Failure to thrive or acute metabolic decompensation is not expected and warrants reassessment
reference.prognosis: Hyperlysinaemia is generally regarded as a benign inborn error of metabolism with a normal life expectancy and no specific morbidity attributable to the biochemical abnormality. The main clinical value of recognising it lies in avoiding unnecessary investigation or treatment once alternative diagnoses have been excluded.
pitfalls: Over-investigating or dietary-restricting an asymptomatic child on the basis of raised lysine alone, when the condition is typically benign
Attributing incidental neurodevelopmental problems to hyperlysinaemia rather than seeking an independent cause
Confusing primary hyperlysinaemia with secondary elevation of lysine in urea cycle disorders or generalised aminoaciduria
Overlooking coexisting saccharopinuria, which arises from the same AASS gene and can cause diagnostic confusion
Assuming the biochemistry implies a glutaric-aciduria-type risk of encephalopathic crisis, which it does not
references: Standard inborn errors of metabolism textbooks
management: Recognise hyperlysinaemia as a generally benign biochemical variant and avoid unnecessary lysine restriction or pharmacotherapy
Confirm the diagnosis biochemically and by AASS genotyping, distinguishing combined enzyme deficiency from isolated saccharopinuria
Actively exclude neurotoxic mimics, especially glutaric aciduria type 1, when a child has neurological symptoms
Reassure the family and prevent an unnecessary diagnostic cascade once alternative causes are excluded
Where developmental or neurological problems coexist, evaluate for an independent coincidental diagnosis rather than attributing them to the metabolic finding
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance
Provide periodic follow-up through a metabolic service to confirm ongoing wellbeing
